newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hesse vote gives Kohl's CDU well-timed boost.
newsitem.headline: Hesse vote gives Kohl's CDU well-timed boost.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, worn down by months of internal squabbling and mounting economic woes, said on Monday they picked up an encouraging and unexpected boost from local elections in Hesse.

Several CDU leaders pointed gleefully to the returns from the affluent western state, where Kohl's party defied national trends and gained one point statewide compared with the last local poll four years ago to 33 percent.

The CDU, which has fallen steeply in national opinion surveys, also leaped 2.9 points in the financial capital of Frankfurt to 36.3 percent, and is now the strongest party in the city that was long a Social Democrat(SPD) bastion. "This was a good stage victory on the way to the federal elections next year," said Peter Hintze, CDU general secretary, at a news conference on Monday in Bonn. "The results show that the public is behind Helmut Kohl's reform programme."

Admitting they had been worried voters would punish them for wrangling over tax increases, rising unemployment and a stagnating economy, several leading Kohl deputies called the modest gains in Hesse an impressive triumph.
The SPD, Kohl's main opponent in Bonn, had openly called upon voters angry about the economy and other woes plaguing the country to send a message to Kohl in the local elections.

"We were in a difficult position there because of the difficult national issues and all the protests against us," said Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl. "But all in all these were very, very positive and uplifting results in Hesse."

Unemployment hit a post-war record of 4.66 million in January and is expected to climb even further to 4.8 million in February, levels last seen in Germany in the months before Adolf Hitler and his Nazi party took power in 1933.
"This is a genuine triumph for the CDU," said Finance Minister Theo Waigel, chairman of the CDU's Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU).

"The CDU's ability to gain despite these difficult circumstances proves that the union is on the right track. If the coalition sticks with its reform course, we have a great chance to win the federal elections next year."
Kohl's CDU has often appeared ruderless in recent months, stumbling from one squabble to another within a coalition which includes its CSU and the centrist Free Democrats (FDP).

A national opinion poll published by the Emnid research institute found the centre-right coalition, bogged down by the fractious in-fighting, would lose to a leftist majority made up of the SPD and Greens if elections were held now.
The poll found the CDU slipping to 36 percent and the FDP receiving six percent compared with 37 percent for the SPD and 10 percent for the Greens.

"Considering the situation we are in right now, I have to say that I am personally very, very pleasantly surprised with the results," said Bohl, in an interview with NDR radio. "And this came in a traditional state stronghold for the SPD."

Bonn observers said that Kohl, who often returns from his annual Easter fasting holiday in Austria with renewed vigour, may have an even greater appetite to tackle reform issues after picking up the tailwind from Hesse.
The vote in Hesse, home to 4.5 million eligible voters, was overshadowed by local issues but carried national implications as one of only two elections this year. Hamburg votes in September.
The SPD also posted modest gains in Hesse, gaining 1.6 points to 38.0 percent compared with the last election in 1993.

The main losers in Hesse were the smaller parties. The environmentalist Greens stagnated at 11 percent while the FDP fell to 4 percent from 5.1 percent and the far-right Republicans dropped to 6.6 percent from 8.3 percent.
